topic: How bread prices fed a revolution

opening.say: Picture a family in Paris in seventeen eighty-nine, where bread was the main food and most of the day's pay went to it.
Say a worker earns a fixed wage, and the price of a loaf keeps climbing after a bad harvest. What gets squeezed?
That fraction is the whole story. When it grows, there's less left for rent, fuel, or anything else at all.

more.say: Suppose a loaf costs one unit and a worker earns four a day. If the family needs two loaves, half the pay is gone.
Now a hailstorm ruins the wheat, and the same loaf costs two units. The same two loaves would take all of the daily pay.
So nothing about the worker changed, not the job, not the hours, only the price. That's why a bad harvest could hit a whole city at once.

plan.setup: Watch the bread share climb as prices rise.
plan.narration: [[wage-line]]Wages stayed flat. [[price-curve]]Then bad harvests pushed the price of bread up. [[share-rises]]So bread swallowed more of every paycheck, [[danger-zone]]until nearly everything went to eating. [[anger-spreads]]Hungry crowds blamed the crown, and that anger helped fuel the revolution.
plan.plan:
wage-line: a flat horizontal line labeled wage stays level across the board.
price-curve: a curve labeled bread price rises steadily above the wage line after a harvest dip marker.
share-rises: a bar showing the share, bread cost divided by wage, filling upward as the curve climbs.
danger-zone: the bar approaches the top and turns red near a full hundred percent of the wage.
anger-spreads: small crowd figures appear around the bar, growing in number as the share stays high.
plan.close: If wages had risen along with prices, would the anger have been the same?
